newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS - BT/MCI Concert rewrites score in telecoms.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - BT/MCI Concert rewrites score in telecoms.

text.p: The telecommunications world found itself dancing to a new beat on Monday after the huge $21 billion trans-Atlantic merger between British Telecommunications Plc and MCI Communications Corp to form Concert Plc.

The largest cross-border takeover in history, toasted with champagne when it was unveiled on Sunday, creates a global powerhouse which vies with American giant AT&T Corp as the second largest in the industry by market capitalisation. Only Japan's Nippon Telegraph and Telephone Corp is larger.
The move will create work aplenty for British, American and European regulators who will spend the coming months poring over the fine print of the deal as they decide whether to clear it.
The BT/MCI merger will spawn a telecoms titan with annual revenues of around $40 billion and 43 million business and residential customers in 70 countries.
For customers, the deal promises better service and lower international calling charges, while for businesses it should mean that the company can support them wherever they are.
It will cause sleepless nights for rival telecoms groups such as AT&T, Sprint Corp, France Telecom and Deutsche Telekom as they ponder how to respond.
Sprint is allied with the French and Germans in the Global One international venture while AT&T is part of a network of alliances called World Partners.
The new company is expected to expand its operations in the Asia-Pacific region -- a long-held BT aim.

It also intends to erode AT&T's dominance in the U.S. long distance market where MCI currently has a 20 percent slice of a $75 billion annual cake. It also aims to build a significant share in the U.S. local market as it is liberalised.

Markets applauded the Concert programme, BT shares adding 22 1/2p to 373 1/2p in very heavy London trading. BT's American depositary shares jumped almost 10 percent after New York opened for business.

Under the terms of the merger BT, which already owns 20 percent of Washington-based MCI, will issue Concert cash and stock for the remaining 80 percent. Holders of MCI stock will end up controlling around a third of the merged company.
The rising value of BT stock in the U.S. increased the value of the offer for MCI to $39 a share or $21.5 billion. MCI shares traded up 3/4 on New York's Nasdaq at $31 on Monday.
BT chief executive Sir Peter Bonfield has said it could take a year for the deal to win regulatory approval.
"There are a lot of hurdles to be cleared but I think the deal will go through," said one London-based share analyst.
BT said on Monday it was optimistic that the European Commission would clear the merger.
British officials have said only that they are looking at the deal. AT&T has already called on the U.S. Federal Communications Commission to give it thorough scrutiny.

The merged company will acquire the nine percent stake which MCI holds in Rupert Murdoch's News Corp media empire. MCI, perhaps wary of regulatory concerns, said on Sunday it did not plan to pursue an option to increase this to 13 percent.
